stem: A developer enables thinking on a current model but leaves the thinking text hidden, since users only need the final answer. The bill shows far more output tokens than the visible answers contain. What explains this?

options.text: Hidden thinking blocks are a display bug, and support can refund the extra output tokens.
options.why: This is expected billing behavior, not a bug.

options.text: Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens even when the thinking text is not returned.
options.why: Display settings only control visibility; the reasoning is still generated and billed as output.

options.text: Hidden thinking is billed at the input rate, which the bill reports inside the output total.
options.why: Thinking is billed as output tokens, not input tokens.

options.text: The API adds a fixed per-request surcharge whenever thinking is enabled on the request.
options.why: There is no flat thinking surcharge; cost comes from the thinking tokens generated.

explanation: Thinking tokens are generated output. Whether the summary is shown or omitted, the reasoning is billed as output tokens and counts toward max_tokens. Budget for it, and use effort to control how much the model thinks.
reference: Claude API docs — Building with thinking

stem: A classification prompt asks Claude to "output the label first, then explain your reasoning." Reviewers notice that the explanations often argue for a label that looks wrong. What change is most likely to improve label accuracy?

options.text: Keep the same order, but ask for a longer and more detailed explanation after the label.
options.why: Reasoning written after the label cannot change the label that was already generated.

options.text: Remove the explanation entirely so the model focuses only on picking the label.
options.why: This removes the rationalization but does not give the model any room to reason before deciding.

options.text: Have the model reason before it commits to a label, such as by enabling thinking.
options.why: Each token depends only on earlier tokens, so reasoning must come before the label to influence it.

options.text: Raise the temperature so the model considers more alternative labels.
options.why: More randomness makes labels less consistent; it does not add reasoning.

explanation: Models generate one token at a time, conditioned on what came before. A label produced first is fixed before any reasoning exists, and later text tends to justify it. Letting the model reason first, through thinking or a reasoning section before the answer, lets that reasoning shape the decision.
reference: Claude docs — Let Claude think (chain of thought)

stem: After enabling adaptive thinking at high effort, some responses stop with stop_reason "max_tokens" and very little answer text. The developer set max_tokens to 1,024 for the old non-thinking version. What should they do?

options.text: Raise max_tokens well above 1,024 (streaming if large), since thinking counts toward it.
options.why: Thinking and the answer share the max_tokens limit, so a small cap is used up before the answer is written.

options.text: Keep max_tokens at 1,024 and add "keep your thinking brief" to the system prompt.
options.why: This may shorten thinking a little but still leaves a cap too small for thinking plus the answer.

options.text: Retry each truncated request until one of the retries happens to finish inside the 1,024 limit.
options.why: Retries repeat the same cost and truncation without fixing the cause.

options.text: Lower the effort to the minimum so no thinking tokens are ever generated.
options.why: Low effort reduces thinking but does not guarantee none, and it may lower quality needlessly.

explanation: With thinking on, max_tokens caps the thinking and the final answer together. Caps tuned for non-thinking responses are usually too small. Set a larger cap (streaming when it is large) and use effort, not the cap, to control how much the model thinks.
reference: Claude API docs — Building with thinking

stem: An internal agent on a current model produces excellent results, but it makes many small tool calls and writes long preambles, so cost and latency are too high. Evals show quality has headroom. What is the best first change?

options.text: Cap max_tokens at a low value so every response is forced to be short.
options.why: A hard cap truncates work mid-task instead of making the agent more efficient.

options.text: Hide the thinking output so fewer tokens are billed on each response.
options.why: Hiding thinking changes visibility only; it is billed the same.

options.text: Move the agent to the smallest model tier and accept whatever quality results.
options.why: A tier change is a bigger, riskier step than tuning effort, and it ignores the quality bar.

options.text: Lower the effort level and confirm on the eval set that quality still holds.
options.why: Lower effort means fewer, more consolidated tool calls and terser output, which targets exactly this waste.

explanation: Effort applies to every output token, including tool calls and preambles. When quality has headroom, lowering effort is usually the simplest cost and latency lever, and should be checked against evals before changing models or imposing hard caps.
reference: Claude API docs — Effort

stem: A prompt includes five examples of release-note summaries. Every example has exactly three bullets and a "Risk:" line. Now every output has three bullets and a "Risk:" line, even for tiny changes with no risk. What is the best fix?

options.text: Vary the examples, including small changes with fewer bullets and no risk line.
options.why: Diverse examples stop the model from copying incidental patterns shared by every example.

options.text: Delete all examples and rely on zero-shot instructions from now on.
options.why: This throws away the format guidance the examples provide instead of fixing their bias.

options.text: Add five more examples in the same style so the pattern is even clearer.
options.why: More examples with the same shape reinforce the unwanted pattern.

options.text: Add "do not copy the examples" at the end of the prompt and keep them as they are.
options.why: The examples still teach the pattern more strongly than a vague instruction removes it.

explanation: Multi-shot examples are powerful, and the model learns from everything they share, including incidental features. Examples should be relevant and diverse enough, covering edge cases, that Claude does not pick up unintended patterns such as fixed lengths or mandatory sections.
reference: Claude docs — Use examples (multishot prompting)

stem: A lending app uses Claude to flag applications for manual review. Auditors must be able to explain any past decision, and re-running an old request sometimes gives a different answer. Which two practices best meet the audit requirement? (Choose two.)

options.text: Store the full request and response for every decision at the time it is made.
options.why: Because output can vary between runs, the record of what actually happened must be captured when it happens.

options.text: Set temperature to 0 so auditors can reproduce any decision by re-running it later.
options.why: Low temperature never guaranteed identical output, and the newest models reject non-default sampling values, so re-running is not an audit trail.

options.text: Pin an exact model ID so that the same model version is recorded for each decision.
options.why: A pinned ID ties each logged decision to a known model and prevents silent changes.

options.text: Route each decision to whichever model is newest on that day, so decisions always use the latest one.
options.why: Changing models over time makes past decisions harder to explain unless each one is tied to a recorded, fixed model.

options.text: Re-run the original prompt during each audit and treat the new output as the decision.
options.why: A new run may differ from the original, so it does not show what was actually decided.

explanation: LLM output is non-deterministic, so reproducibility cannot rely on re-running. For audits, record the exact inputs, outputs, and pinned model version at decision time, and treat that record as the source of truth.
reference: Claude docs — Models overview; Increase output consistency

stem: A streaming chat UI moved to a current model with thinking on. Users now see a long blank pause before any text and assume the app has hung. Answer quality must not drop. What should the developer do?

options.text: Disable thinking so the answer text starts streaming right away.
options.why: This removes the pause but gives up the reasoning quality the requirement protects.

options.text: Switch the UI to non-streaming so users see the whole answer at once.
options.why: Users would wait even longer with no feedback at all.

options.text: Request summarized thinking and show it, or a progress state, while it runs.
options.why: The pause is thinking that is hidden by default; showing summaries or progress keeps the quality and reassures users.

options.text: Lower max_tokens so that the model spends less time thinking before it answers.
options.why: A lower cap risks truncated answers rather than making thinking visible.

explanation: On many current models, thinking is returned with its text omitted by default, so a streaming UI sees thinking blocks with no visible text before the answer. Opting into summarized thinking, or showing a progress state, fixes the experience without reducing quality.
reference: Claude API docs — Building with thinking

stem: A developer needs Anthropic support to investigate one specific failed API call from yesterday. The app logs the prompt, the timestamp, and the error message. What else should the app have logged to make this fast?

options.text: The full API key, so support can look up the account that made the call.
options.why: Keys are secrets and must never be logged or shared.

options.text: The client machine hostname, so support can trace the network path.
options.why: Support identifies API calls by request ID, not by client hostname.

options.text: The SDK version, which support uses as the unique key for each call.
options.why: SDK version can help with context but does not identify a single request.

options.text: The request ID returned with every response and error.
options.why: Every response carries a unique request-id, which is what support uses to find a specific call.

explanation: Every API response includes a unique request ID (the request-id header, also in error bodies, and exposed by the SDKs). Logging it with each call makes support investigations and your own trace analysis straightforward.
reference: Claude API docs — Errors (request ID)

stem: A service streams responses and treats any request that returns HTTP 200 as a success. During busy periods, some users get answers that stop abruptly with no error logged. Which two changes should the developer make? (Choose two.)

options.text: Handle error events, such as overloaded, that can arrive in the stream after the 200.
options.why: With streaming, the status is sent before generation, so later failures appear as error events in the stream.

options.text: Assume the truncation comes from the browser, since HTTP 200 guarantees completion.
options.why: A 200 on a stream only means the stream started, not that it finished.

options.text: Raise max_tokens, since the model probably hit its context window without reporting it.
options.why: Context and length limits are reported through stop reasons, and this does not explain silent busy-period failures.

options.text: Turn off streaming during busy periods, because the SDK silently drops streams when the API is busy.
options.why: The SDK does not discard streams; the gap is unhandled error events, and turning off streaming just hides it.

options.text: Treat a stream as complete only when it ends normally with a stop reason.
options.why: A stream that ends without its final events and stop reason did not finish, and should be retried or reported.

explanation: In a streaming response the HTTP status is returned before generation, so errors that happen later (for example overloaded_error) are sent as error events in the stream. Handle those events (or the SDK exceptions they raise), and only treat a stream as successful when it ends normally with a stop reason.
reference: Claude API docs — Streaming messages (error events)

stem: A backend wraps SDK calls in one catch-all handler that checks whether the error message contains "rate". It sometimes retries malformed requests and sometimes fails to retry overloads. What is the better approach?

options.text: Catch the SDK typed errors by class or status, and retry only retryable ones.
options.why: Typed errors separate rate limits and overloads from bad requests reliably.

options.text: Retry every error the same number of times, since the API decides which ones succeed.
options.why: Retrying non-retryable errors such as 400s wastes calls and delays the real fix.

options.text: Match more keywords in the message text, such as "overloaded" and "invalid".
options.why: Message text is not a stable contract, so string matching stays fragile.

options.text: Disable the SDK retries and log every error for a person to retry by hand.
options.why: Manual retries do not scale and throw away the built-in backoff for transient errors.

explanation: The SDKs raise typed exceptions (for example a rate-limit error, an authentication error, a bad-request error) with a status code. Branch on those, most specific first, so transient failures (429, 5xx, 529) are retried and client errors (400, 401, 404) are fixed rather than retried.
reference: Claude API docs — Errors; Client SDKs

stem: A user-facing endpoint must answer or fail within 20 seconds. It uses the SDK with its default settings, which include a long timeout and automatic retries. Occasionally a request hangs for many minutes. Which two changes best meet the requirement? (Choose two.)

options.text: Set a per-request timeout that fits the 20-second budget.
options.why: The default timeout is far longer than the budget, so the endpoint needs its own limit.

options.text: Increase max retries so a hung request is more likely to succeed on a later attempt.
options.why: Timeouts are retried, so more retries multiply the worst-case wait.

options.text: Limit retries so that timeout times attempts stays within the budget, then return a fallback.
options.why: Total wall-clock can reach the timeout multiplied by the number of attempts, so both must fit the budget.

options.text: Switch to the Message Batches API so long requests no longer block the endpoint.
options.why: Batches are asynchronous and far too slow for a 20-second interactive response.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so the model finishes in fewer, larger responses.
options.why: A larger output cap can make individual requests longer, not shorter.

explanation: SDK defaults suit long generations, not tight user-facing budgets. Because timed-out requests are retried, worst-case latency is roughly the timeout times the number of attempts. Set a per-request timeout and a retry count that fit the budget, and degrade gracefully when they are exceeded.
reference: Claude API docs — Client SDKs (timeouts and retries)

stem: A web app generates long reports that take up to five minutes. Its serverless functions must respond within 60 seconds, and users wait on a progress page. Which design best fits?

options.text: Submit each report to the Message Batches API and have the progress page poll the batch.
options.why: Batches can take much longer than five minutes, which does not suit a user waiting on the page.

options.text: Make a single non-streaming call inside the function and raise max_tokens to finish faster.
options.why: The call would still outlast the 60-second limit, and a larger cap does not speed it up.

options.text: Have the browser call the Messages API directly with a key so no function limit applies.
options.why: This exposes the API key to every user.

options.text: Enqueue a job for a worker that streams from the API, and have the page poll the job status.
options.why: A background worker is not bound by the 60-second limit, streaming avoids idle timeouts, and polling your own job store is cheap.

explanation: When generation outlasts a request/response limit, move it to a background worker and let the client poll (or subscribe to) job status. The worker should stream long generations. Batches suit latency-tolerant bulk work, and direct browser calls leak credentials.
reference: Claude API docs — Streaming messages; Errors (long requests)

stem: A developer streams responses that include tool calls. Their code runs JSON.parse on each input_json_delta chunk as it arrives and frequently throws parse errors. What should they do?

options.text: Switch off streaming for all requests that include tools, since the two features cannot be combined.
options.why: Streaming works with tools; the parsing approach is the problem.

options.text: Accumulate each block's partial JSON and parse it when the block stops, or use SDK helpers.
options.why: Each delta is a fragment of a JSON string, so it is only valid once the block is complete.

options.text: Catch the parse errors and skip any chunk that fails, keeping only the chunks that parse.
options.why: Skipping fragments corrupts the tool input.

options.text: Ask the model in the prompt to emit each tool argument as a separate complete JSON object.
options.why: Prompting cannot change how the stream splits tool input into partial strings.

explanation: When streaming, tool_use input arrives as partial JSON string deltas. Concatenate them per content block and parse once the block ends, or let the SDK helpers assemble the final message for you.
reference: Claude API docs — Streaming messages

stem: The same service runs in development, staging, and production. Production must send traffic through an internal API gateway, and finance wants spend reported separately per environment. How should the developer configure the SDK client?

options.text: Add if-statements in code that pick the key and gateway URL from constants for each environment.
options.why: Hard-coded keys in code are a security risk, and code branches per environment are error-prone.

options.text: Use one shared API key everywhere and tag each request with its environment in the prompt text.
options.why: Prompt text is not a billing dimension, and a shared key mixes the environments.

options.text: Load a separate key and the base URL from each environment's config and secret store.
options.why: Per-environment keys separate usage, and environment-driven config sends production through the gateway without code changes.

options.text: Route development and staging through the production gateway too, so all traffic looks the same.
options.why: This mixes environments and still does not separate spend.

explanation: Keep one code path and configure the client from the environment: the API key from a secret store, and a base URL override where traffic must go through a gateway. Separate keys (or workspaces) per environment make usage and spend reportable per environment.
reference: Claude API docs — Client SDKs; Workspaces

stem: A team is building an agent that performs complex, multi-file refactors in a large codebase overnight. Correctness matters most, speed does not, and the budget is flexible. Which model tier is the best starting point?

options.text: Haiku, because its low per-token price allows many retries overnight.
options.why: Retries do not replace the capability that complex refactors require.

options.text: Opus, the tier built for complex, long-running agentic coding.
options.why: Hard, long-horizon coding where correctness matters most is a core use case for Opus; start capability-first and optimize later.

options.text: Sonnet with thinking disabled, to keep each overnight run predictable.
options.why: Disabling thinking reduces reasoning on exactly the kind of task that needs it.

options.text: Haiku with fast mode enabled to finish the overnight work sooner.
options.why: Speed is not the constraint here, and fast mode is offered on supported Opus models, not Haiku.

explanation: Opus targets complex, long-running agentic coding and knowledge work, Sonnet balances capability with speed and cost, and Haiku suits fast, high-volume, simpler tasks. When correctness dominates and latency and cost are flexible, start capability-first and tune effort or tier down later based on evals.
reference: Claude docs — Choosing a model

stem: A customer assistant must handle moderately complex questions with tool use at high volume. In evals, Haiku fails many multi-step questions, while Opus passes but exceeds the budget and latency targets. What should the developer try next?

options.text: Keep Haiku and add more instructions until the multi-step questions pass.
options.why: The evals show a capability gap that more instructions are unlikely to close.

options.text: Ship Opus anyway, since passing evals matters more than the stated targets.
options.why: This ignores explicit budget and latency requirements.

options.text: Alternate between Haiku and Opus at random to average out cost and quality.
options.why: Random routing gives inconsistent quality without targeting the hard questions.

options.text: Evaluate Sonnet, the tier that balances capability, speed, and cost.
options.why: Sonnet sits between the two tiers and is the natural candidate when one is too weak and the other too costly.

explanation: Model selection weighs quality, latency, and cost. When the smallest tier misses the quality bar and the largest misses cost and latency targets, the balanced middle tier is the next thing to measure on the same eval.
reference: Claude docs — Choosing a model

stem: An app runs on an Opus-tier model at its default effort. Quality is great, but latency and cost are over target, and the team plans to move to Haiku, which failed some evals last quarter. What is the best first step?

options.text: Measure the current model at lower effort, alongside smaller tiers, on the same eval set.
options.why: Lowering effort is often a better lever than switching models and keeps quality the team already trusts.

options.text: Move to Haiku now, since the newest Haiku must have fixed last quarter's failures.
options.why: Assuming improvements without measuring risks shipping a regression.

options.text: Add a cascade that tries Haiku first and falls back to Opus when answers look weak.
options.why: A cascade adds complexity and double calls before simpler options have been measured.

options.text: Stay on Opus and cut max_tokens in half to reduce both latency and cost.
options.why: A lower cap risks truncated answers without reducing the work the model does.

explanation: Effort trades thoroughness for latency and cost within a single model, and is often a better lever than switching models. Measure lower effort on the current model against smaller tiers on the same eval before building cascades or migrating.
reference: Claude docs — Choosing a model; Effort

stem: After upgrading to a newer model, an agent calls its search tool on almost every turn. The system prompt, written for an older model, says "CRITICAL: You MUST use the search tool whenever in doubt." Which two actions should the team take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Soften the wording to plain guidance such as "Use the search tool when the answer needs current data."
options.why: Newer models respond more strongly to system prompts, so emphatic language written for older models causes overtriggering.

options.text: Roll back to the older model permanently, since newer models cannot follow tool instructions.
options.why: The newer model follows instructions closely; the prompt is what needs updating.

options.text: Re-run the eval suite after the prompt change to confirm tool use is appropriate.
options.why: Behavior changes across releases should be verified with evals, not assumed fixed.

options.text: Add an even stronger rule telling the model it must never overuse the search tool.
options.why: Stacking emphatic rules adds conflict instead of removing the cause.

options.text: Remove the search tool from the request so it cannot be overused.
options.why: This breaks the cases that genuinely need search.

explanation: Model releases can change behavior without any API change. Newer models follow system prompts more closely, so aggressive wording that helped older models undertrigger less can now cause overtriggering. Dial back the language and verify with evals as part of migration.
reference: Claude docs — Prompting best practices; Model migration guide

stem: A router sends simple requests to a Haiku model and hard ones to an Opus model, using identical request parameters for both, including adaptive thinking. The Haiku model in use does not support adaptive thinking, and those requests fail. What is the best fix?

options.text: Send every request to Opus so that one parameter set works everywhere.
options.why: This avoids the error by giving up the cost and latency benefit of routing.

options.text: Catch the error on Haiku requests and retry them unchanged after a short delay.
options.why: An unsupported parameter fails the same way on every retry.

options.text: Build request parameters per model, based on each model's documented capabilities.
options.why: Models differ in supported features, so the router must send each one a configuration it accepts.

options.text: Remove thinking from all requests, including Opus, so the parameters match.
options.why: This throws away reasoning quality on the hard requests that need it.

explanation: Feature support, such as adaptive thinking, differs across models and tiers. Multi-model systems should build per-model request settings from documented capabilities (the models documentation or the Models API) rather than one shared parameter set.
reference: Claude docs — Models overview; Adaptive thinking

stem: A multi-turn support chat resends the whole growing conversation on every turn and wants to use prompt caching to cut input cost. Where should the cache breakpoint go?

options.text: On the first user message only, since it is the part that never changes.
options.why: This caches only a tiny prefix and misses the growing history that is resent each turn.

options.text: On the last block of the latest turn, or use automatic caching.
options.why: Marking the end of the newest turn lets the next request read the whole prior conversation from cache.

options.text: Nowhere, because prompt caching works only for system prompts, not messages.
options.why: Message content can be cached; conversation history is a common target.

options.text: On a timestamp block at the start of each request so the cache stays fresh.
options.why: A changing value at the start of the prompt invalidates everything after it.

explanation: For multi-turn conversations, place the breakpoint on the last block of the most recent turn (or use top-level automatic caching, which does this for you). Each new request then reads the previous conversation prefix from cache and only pays full price for the new tail.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompt caching

stem: A report generator's token logs show that output tokens make up most of its spend. Reports are often three times longer than readers need. Which change will reduce cost most directly?

options.text: Shorten the system prompt, since input tokens drive most of the bill.
options.why: The logs show output dominates, and output tokens cost several times more than input tokens.

options.text: Set a low max_tokens so each report is cut off at the target length.
options.why: A hard cap truncates reports mid-section instead of making them concise.

options.text: State the target length and structure in the prompt, then check quality.
options.why: Output is the expensive side; asking for the length and format readers need removes unneeded output.

options.text: Enable prompt caching on the report template to lower the cost of output.
options.why: Caching reduces input cost only; it does not change output tokens.

explanation: Output tokens are priced higher than input tokens, so verbose responses often dominate cost. Use usage data to see where spend goes, then constrain output length and format in the prompt (and tune effort) rather than truncating with max_tokens.
reference: Claude docs — Pricing; Be clear and direct

stem: An agent adds or removes tools depending on the user's current mode. Usage logs show cache_creation_input_tokens close to the full prompt size on most requests and almost no cache reads. What is the best fix?

options.text: Move the breakpoint later in the conversation so more content is cached each turn.
options.why: Tools come first in the prompt, so changing them still invalidates everything after.

options.text: Keep one stable tool list and pass the current mode in message content.
options.why: Tools render first, so any change to the tool set invalidates the whole cache; a stable tool list keeps the prefix reusable.

options.text: Switch to the 1-hour TTL so that cache entries survive mode changes.
options.why: TTL does not help when the cached prefix itself changes.

options.text: Create a separate cache breakpoint for each mode's set of tools.
options.why: Each mode still starts from a different prefix, so switching modes keeps missing.

explanation: Caching is a prefix match rendered as tools, then system, then messages. Changing the tool set changes the very start of the prompt, so every mode switch forces a full rewrite. Keep tools stable and express modes through message content; usage fields reveal this pattern.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompt caching

stem: A nightly Message Batches job sends 20,000 requests that share a 30,000-token instruction prefix. The team wants to add prompt caching and forecast savings. Which two statements should shape the plan? (Choose two.)

options.text: Batches can take longer than five minutes, so the 1-hour cache TTL is likely to give better hit rates.
options.why: Batch processing can outlast the default 5-minute lifetime, so a longer TTL keeps shared entries alive.

options.text: Prompt caching cannot be used inside a batch, so the prefix will be billed in full every time.
options.why: Batches support prompt caching, and the discounts can stack.

options.text: Cache hits in batches are best effort, so the forecast should assume a partial hit rate.
options.why: Batch requests run concurrently and in any order, so not every request will read from cache.

options.text: Results come back in submission order, so the first request is guaranteed to warm the cache for the rest.
options.why: Batch requests are processed in any order, and results must be matched by custom_id.

options.text: The batch discount replaces caching savings, so only one of the two can apply to a request.
options.why: The batch discount and caching discounts can stack.

explanation: Batches and prompt caching work together and their discounts can stack. Because batches can run longer than five minutes and requests are processed concurrently and in any order, use the 1-hour TTL for shared context and forecast with a conservative, best-effort hit rate.
reference: Claude API docs — Message Batches (prompt caching)

stem: A team is forecasting the cost of moving a workload to a newer model with thinking enabled. Their draft reuses last year's token counts from the old model and multiplies them by the new prices. What is the best way to improve the forecast?

options.text: Keep the old counts, since tokenizers and output lengths stay the same across releases.
options.why: Tokenizers can change between models, and thinking adds output tokens the old counts never had.

options.text: Add a flat 10% margin to the draft to cover any differences between the models.
options.why: An arbitrary margin is a guess, not a measurement of the new model.

options.text: Forecast only input tokens, since thinking tokens are free when their text is hidden.
options.why: Thinking is billed as output whether or not its text is returned.

options.text: Pilot a sample on the new model, counting input and reading usage for output.
options.why: Measured counts from the target model capture tokenizer and thinking changes that old numbers miss.

explanation: Token counts are model-specific, and enabling thinking adds billed output. Re-baseline with the token counting endpoint on the target model and run a representative pilot, reading usage fields to measure real output and thinking, and ideally express the result as cost per completed task.
reference: Claude API docs — Token counting; Building with thinking
